idea.body: A multiplication fact is just equal groups counted fast. 6 times 7 means 6 groups of 7, or a rectangle 6 tiles by 7 tiles, which always comes out to 42. Learn a fact cold and three more facts come free. 7 times 6 is the same 42 turned sideways, and 42 divided by 6 or by 7 undoes it. Doubling a known fact gives a new one fast: knowing 4 times 7 is 28 means 8 times 7 is double that, 56. Facts up to 12 times 12 are worth knowing so well that you never have to count groups one at a time again.

figure.alt: A grid of 6 rows and 7 columns, all cells filled, showing 6 times 7.

workedExample.prompt: A robot's tile arm lays 8 rows of 6 tiles. How many tiles does it lay in total?
steps: 8 rows of 6 tiles is 8 groups of 6.
You already know 4 times 6 is 24.
8 is double 4, so double the product too: double 24 is 48.
The robot lays 48 tiles.

ways.name: Equal-groups array
ways.when: Use this when you can picture the fact as rows and columns.
steps: Picture 6 rows of 7 dots, one row for each group.
Count the dots in one row: 7.
There are 6 equal rows.
6 groups of 7 is the same as 6 times 7.
6 times 7 is 42.
ways.trap: Miscounting a row or column by one, giving a product off by a whole group.

figure.alt: 6 rows, each a strip of 7 equal-group dots, filling in one row at a time to show 6 times 7 is 42.

frames.caption: Count the dots in one row: 7.

ways.name: Doubling a known fact
ways.when: Use this when the fact you need is double a fact you already know.
steps: Think of a fact you already know that is half of the one you need: 4 times 7 is 28.
8 is double 4, so 8 times 7 uses twice as many groups.
Double the known product: double 28.
Double of 28 is 56.
ways.trap: Doubling the group size but forgetting to also double the product.

ways.name: Skip counting
ways.when: Use this when you can count up by the group size without losing track.
steps: Count the group size up, one jump per group: 9, 18, 27, 36, 45.
Each jump adds one more group of 9.
Stop once the number of jumps matches the number of groups: 5 jumps.
The last number reached is the product.
ways.trap: Losing count of which jump you are on and stopping one jump early.

ways.name: Nearby ten fact
ways.when: Use this when one factor sits close to 10.
steps: Multiply by 10 instead, an easy fact: 10 times 6 is 60.
9 groups is one group fewer than 10 groups.
Subtract one group's worth from the ten-fact: subtract 6.
60 minus 6 is 54.
ways.trap: Subtracting the multiplier instead of the group size.

bank.prompt: On a comic shop's display rack: 12 x 9, 11 x 10, 8 x 13, 12 x 8, 9 x 11. Order these products from least to greatest.
explanation: Work out each product first.
The products are 108, 110, 104, 96, 99 in that order.
From least to greatest: 96, 99, 104, 108, 110.
bank.useAgain: when several multiplication facts need to be lined up by size.
hints: Compute every product before comparing them.
Compare the actual products, not how the expressions look.
bank.socraticHint: Can a bigger-looking expression ever have a smaller product?

stretch.prompt: How many whole-number factor pairs does 40 have, counting a pair like 1 and 40 once?
explanation: List every pair of whole numbers that multiply to 40: 1 and 40, 2 and 20, 4 and 10, 5 and 8.
That is 4 pairs in total.
stretch.useAgain: when you need every way two whole numbers can multiply to a given target.
hints: Start from 1 and work up, checking which numbers divide evenly into it.
Stop once your two numbers in a pair cross over each other.
stretch.socraticHint: Once you find a factor bigger than its matching pair, have you already found it before?

variant.prompt: How many whole-number factor pairs does 72 have, counting a pair like 1 and 72 once?

stretch.prompt: Which of these numbers has an ODD number of whole-number factors: 24, 36, 48, 60?
explanation: Factors usually come in pairs, which makes an even count.
A perfect square has one factor that pairs with itself, so its count is odd.
36 is the perfect square here, so it has an odd number of factors.
stretch.useAgain: when you need to spot a perfect square by its factor count instead of counting every factor.
hints: Factors pair up, except for one special kind of number.
Check which of the choices is a perfect square.
stretch.socraticHint: Why would a perfect square be the one number whose factors do not all pair up differently?

explanation: Multiply in: 4, running total 4.
Multiply in: 5, running total 20.
Multiply in: 6, running total 120.
stretch.useAgain: when three or more numbers need to be multiplied together in a chain.
hints: Multiply two factors first, then multiply that result by the next factor.
Multiply them in any order; the final product stays the same.
stretch.socraticHint: Does the order you multiply the factors in change the final product?

stretch.prompt: I am a number between 10 and 99. I am a perfect square. My digits multiply to 10. What number am I?
explanation: List the perfect squares between 10 and 99.
Check each one's digit product against the clue.
Only 25 has digits that multiply to 10.
stretch.useAgain: when a number is described by more than one clue and you need to narrow it down.
hints: List every perfect square in the range before checking the digit clue.
Multiply each candidate's digits together and compare to the target.
stretch.socraticHint: Why check the square clue before the digit-product clue instead of the other way around?

stretch.prompt: On a bakery cart's muffin trays, a rectangle of tiles is 6 rows tall. It is split into a 6 by 4 part and a 6 by 9 part, side by side. What is the total number of tiles?
explanation: The first part is 6 times 4, which is 24.
The second part is 6 times 9, which is 54.
24 plus 54 is 78.
stretch.useAgain: when a big array is easier to count as two smaller arrays added together.
hints: Find each part's tile count separately first.
Add the two parts together for the whole rectangle.
stretch.socraticHint: Would 6 times 13 give you the same total in one step?
